title: Longreads + Open Thread
gist: Byrne Hobart's weekly longreads: AI-driven election disinformation was a non-event (and red-teaming made LLMs more robust), dual-class protections are wrong when they shield an executive like Jensen Huang from personal/sanctions-related oversight, and 19th-century newspaper economics (cheap printing, postal subsidies, ad-funded boilerplate syndication) mirror today's internet media cycles.

insights.claim: Byrne Hobart argues AI-generated political disinformation had little electoral impact in 2026 because fakes are only believable when close to reality and most voters' views are already polarized.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Discount 'deepfake election' risk narratives when sizing regulatory or content-moderation themes.
insights.locator: Caucus.AI reports on the impact AI

insights.claim: Trump is effectively disinformation-proof because his own norm-breaking, attention-seeking statements outcompete anything a deepfaker could invent.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Synthetic-media threats are weakest against candidates whose real statements are already maximally outrageous.
insights.quote: Inventing funny or outrageous Trump statements is one of those jobs where humans still beat the bots.
insights.locator: Caucus.AI reports on the impact AI

insights.claim: Researchers who created fake campaign sites for real politicians and fictional races found LLMs cited those sites, showing LLMs themselves can be fooled by disinformation.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: LLM answer-engines are an attack surface for SEO-style manipulation — relevant for AI search vendors' trust/safety spend.
insights.locator: The piece has much more, including one case

insights.claim: Hobart frames AI red-teaming of LLM source-citation as security-enhancing: once fake-site tactics enter LLMs' world models, models work harder to cite official sources.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Expect adversarial testing to steadily harden AI search against known manipulation patterns.
insights.locator: But this is a case where AI-driven red-teaming

insights.claim: Modern US conservatives appear more willing than the left to socialize with broadly aligned people who disagree on key issues, as seen at the launch of The Elephant, a conservative publication that takes AI risk seriously.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: AI-safety ideas may gain traction on the right via niche outlets read by staffers, shifting future AI policy.
insights.locator: Chloe Pingeon on visiting the launch party

insights.claim: Publications that frame issue X for a movement indifferent or hostile to X can shift policy indirectly by reaching staffers, editorial writers and coverage editors, even if they don't change party platforms directly.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Track niche ideological outlets as leading indicators of policy-coalition shifts on AI regulation.
insights.locator: But, per the piece above

insights.claim: Hobart argues the 2026 US socialist upsurge is weaker than headlines suggest: newly elected socialists mostly replaced other Democrats, and Angie Nixon outperformed Harris by a smaller margin than other Florida Democrats running statewide.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Don't over-price a leftward policy lurch from 2026 results; the statistics are weaker than the narrative.
insights.quote: the story gets weaker if you dig into the statistics but the high-level headline gets the base excited
insights.locator: In The New Yorker, Jill Lepore

insights.claim: Executive firing protections like dual-class stock are justified when they let a leader make contrarian long-term capital allocation decisions that shareholders hate now but value in a decade.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Evaluate dual-class structures by whether they protect strategic contrarianism, not personal conduct.
insights.locator: In general, you want an executive

insights.claim: Hobart argues the protection around reinstating Jensen Huang shields him precisely from personal-life and sanctions-violation trouble — exactly the cases where an executive should be easy to fire.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Governance discount risk for Nvidia: a board overseeing a CEO immune to oversight on conduct and sanctions issues.
insights.quote: that's exactly when you don't want an executive to be hard to fire
insights.locator: A ReadHaus reader asks for more

insights.claim: A board overseeing a legendary but oversight-immune CEO runs risks that can outweigh the CEO's managerial track record.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Key-person and governance risk should be priced separately from operating excellence.
insights.locator: The risk the board runs

insights.claim: Hobart notes heavy users of Claude Code are temporarily better at judging literary merit of short fiction than literary-prize judges, in the context of a Capital Gains piece debunking claimed flaws of AI-text detection.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: AI-detection tooling may be more reliable than critics claim — relevant to edtech/publishing integrity vendors.
insights.locator: In Capital Gains, a look at what people

insights.claim: GTA VI is less cartoonish than earlier entries because better graphics and an aging audience (former San Andreas players now parents) make stories about economically precarious parents more relatable.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Franchise maturing with its core demographic supports durable engagement for Rockstar's flagship IP.
insights.locator: Joseph Bernstein reviews GTA VI

insights.claim: Parasite load is an underrated driver of Malthusian dynamics: calorie surpluses merely feed microbes and worms unless societies develop countermeasures like clean water and safe food.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Sanitation and antiparasitic interventions are high-ROI development levers; heavily parasitized populations can also point to new drug discoveries.
insights.locator: In Core Memory, Brendan Borrell

insights.claim: A Brief History of Intelligence explains brain evolution computationally, showing a simple steering algorithm (go straight if the food smell strengthens, turn if it weakens) lets a few neurons make a hunter's success inevitable.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Useful mental model for how minimal agentic architectures scale — relevant to robotics/agent design.
insights.locator: But once a living thing can steer itself

insights.claim: Brain research and AI cross-pollinate: Rich Sutton's temporal-difference learning later helped explain dopamine, while hierarchical sensory processing was found in the brain and then applied to artificial neural networks.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Neuroscience remains a source of architectural ideas for AI labs (e.g. video/experience-based learning).
insights.locator: There's some back-and-forth between brain research

insights.claim: The brain's hierarchical prediction architecture means intent and action circuits are tightly coupled, so damage to the motor cortex for an action can impair explaining why someone would perform it.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Supports the thesis that world-modeling and action models should be trained jointly.
insights.locator: This kind of hierarchical model stacks tools

insights.claim: Hobart highlights that the book's author runs an AI company rather than being a trained neuroscientist, arguing AI makes human knowledge more accessible and this is the best era for autodidacts.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: AI lowers the barrier to cross-domain synthesis — a tailwind for small expert teams and independent researchers.
insights.quote: Now is the best time in history for people who love to figure things out.
insights.locator: One last note on this book

insights.claim: In the 19th century, the US government subsidized newspapers heavily, including free postage for newspapers exchanging copies, at a cost of up to 0.2% of GDP.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Distribution subsidies historically shaped media market structure — a precedent for platform/distribution policy debates.
insights.locator: One steady influence was the US government

insights.claim: Cheap printing plus free postage produced an 1860s–1880s boom of low-circulation, often teenage-written newspapers that mostly covered each other — almost exactly like the early blogosphere — until the Post Office tightened the definition of a newspaper.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Low barriers + subsidized distribution create creator booms that end when the distributor changes rules — analogous to platform algorithm shifts.
insights.locator: The definition of a "newspaper" inevitably

insights.claim: Syndicated boilerplate printing plates became most profitable when given away free bundled with ads, often for patent medicines — the same ad-funded model, with the same pull toward sleazy ads, that exists online today.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Free-content-plus-ads networks structurally drift toward low-quality advertisers; watch ad-quality as a margin vs. brand-safety trade-off.
insights.locator: Syndication also turns out to have a strange history

insights.claim: Linotype ended the small-paper era because it made massive print runs for large areas cheaper than small runs for a few towns: low fixed-cost printing enabled entry, low marginal-cost printing favored consolidation.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Technology that lowers marginal rather than fixed costs tends to favor scale incumbents — a lens for AI media economics.
insights.quote: What low fixed-cost printing gives, low marginal-cost printing takes away
insights.locator: What low fixed-cost printing gives

insights.claim: Media careers have returned to technical apprenticeships: as in early printing where typesetters became writers, today indie publications benefit from knowing deliverability, shareable headlines and how search engines work.
insights.speaker: @ByrneHobart
insights.so_what: Technical distribution skill is a moat for independent publishers.
insights.locator: In the early days of printing
